fragment.para: The macro mechanism allows using and defining string macros.

section.title: Using macros
section.para: A reference to a parameter can be done in two different ways:
Both will result in the text of the macro. To stop macro expansion, double the first curly brace.
Referencing macros can be done in text nodes and attribute values. If the macro does not exist, an error will be raised.
Watch out: it is possible that the software that uses the macro mechanism limits where macros can be used!

section.title: Macro expansion flags
section.para: A macro reference can be followed by zero or more flags, separated by colons (:). Assume for instance that the macro called REF contains the value {$REF}. Then referring to it as ${{REF:uc} results in {$REF:uc} (everything upper-case). Referring to is as ${{REF:uc:fns} will result in {$REF:uc:fns} (everything upper-case, filename-safe).

entry.para: Capitalize the macro value (first character upper-case, rest as-is).
Filename safe expansion: replace all forbidden characters in a filename with underscores (_).
Filename safe expansion extra: like the fns flag, additionally replace all whitespace characters with underscores.
Normalize the macro value (like the normalize-space() function).

section.title: Defining macros
section.para: Macros can be defined using the macrodefs element. Where this element can appear depends on the application that uses the macro mechanism and must be defined in its schema. It is always the first child element of some other element (usually for something grouping/container like, for instance sections).

attribute.name: name
attribute.para: The name of the macro. Convention is to use all upper-case.

attribute.name: value
attribute.para: The value for the macro. Can contain nested references to other macros.
